title: Ashtpadi 3, salok: many scriptures
hookLine: I have searched many scriptures; none equals the Name (Sukhmani 3)

cards: Shelves to the ceiling. Notes in every margin. A reader with an answer to every question you could ask.
A person like that can teach a great deal. And then there's the other kind: someone who has read very little, yet carries a steadiness the reader doesn't.
A grandmother who knew three prayers by heart and lived every one of them. Sikh tradition remembers Guru Arjan, the author of Sukhmani, as the Guru who gathered the hymns of the Adi Granth.
And the third ashtpadi opens with a surprising thing for a compiler of scripture to say.

teach.b: Here is the salok: bahu saasatr bahu simritee pekhe sarab dhadhol. Word by word. Bahu: many.
Saasatr: the shastras, the learned treatises of Guru Arjan's world. Simritee: the smritis, the remembered law-books and traditions. Pekhe: I have looked at.
Sarab dhadhol: searched through them all. Then the second line: poojas naahee har hare, Naanak naam amol. In paraphrase: they do not equal God, Har, Har; Nanak, the Name is priceless.
Amol means beyond price, something no money could buy. Notice who's speaking. Not someone who dismisses books without opening them.
Someone who says, I have looked, I've searched them all: a scholar, not a scorner.
And what he found is that the books point beyond themselves. Learning can describe the Name, but it can't be the Name. Read this way, the salok isn't against study.
The Guru Granth Sahib is itself a book, and Sikhs read from it and sing from it.
The salok is about the difference between knowing about God and remembering God. Learning about water is not drinking it.
Some readers hear the line as just as true of their own scripture: reading the Guru Granth Sahib without remembering the One it points to would miss the point too.
Over the next days, the third ashtpadi's stanzas run through a long list of religious efforts, and set each beside the Name.

how: Sikhs reading Sukhmani recite this salok at the start of the third ashtpadi; Sikh teachers cite it when speaking of the difference between scholarship and lived remembrance of the Name.

o: rare, found only in old scripture
priceless, beyond what money could buy
heavy, too weighty to lift alone

games.q: the third salok, word by word — tap the pairs.

s: the salok dismisses books without reading them
its voice says: I have looked, I have searched them all.
some readers hear the salok as applying to Sikh scripture too
reading without remembering misses the point, whatever the book.

games.q: you've searched every learned treatise and law-book of your day. what does the third salok say you find?
o: that none of them equals God, and the Name is priceless.
games.why: bahu saasatr bahu simritee pekhe sarab dhadhol: searched them all, and the Name is amol, beyond price.

practice: Choose one line you know, from Sukhmani, from Japji, or from anything that matters to you; if nothing comes, use this: Nanak, the Name is priceless.
Say it once at normal speed, then at half speed, then one word per breath, and let the last word rest. If you pray, add Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Amol, priceless: Sukhmani's third section, whose salok says, I have searched many shastras and smritis, and none equals God; Nanak, the Name is priceless.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: amol, priceless; the salok's last word for the Name.

carryVoice: Your line: nothing equals the name. He searched them all, and came back to the Name. See you tomorrow.
